verdicts.why: Conveying someone to a place is plain description; no attitude toward the person or the place rides on the verb.
Undergoing or feeling something (take delight, take offence) is neutral framing; the judgement, if any, lives in the object, not in 'take'.
Making use of or accepting something for a purpose (take the opportunity) describes an act without approving or disparaging it.
Occupying or taking on (take one's seat, take up an abode) is bare description with no stance toward what is occupied.
An adult male named plainly; the approval or dislike in the sentences comes entirely from 'agreeable', 'charming', 'gentlemanlike', not from 'man'.
The generic use is dated and some readers find it exclusionary, but that is a register and usage matter; the word takes no attitude toward the human beings it refers to.

'Her man' for a husband or lover is informal and carries a proprietary warmth that 'husband' or 'partner' lacks, but I cannot settle whether that is attitude toward the referent or only colloquial register.
A plain degree adverb; it scales whatever it modifies without adding approval or contempt of its own.
A strong intensifier is a strong meaning, not an attitude; 'much better' judges nothing beyond the comparison it amplifies.
'Pretty much the same' hedges a degree of sameness for all practical purposes; it is a measure, not a judgement.
'Own' after a possessive only sharpens whose something is; the emphasis carries no approval or dismissal of the possessor or the thing.
The mass-noun quantifier ('little difficulty', 'said little') measures amount and nothing else.
'Limited or below average in number or quantity' is size and count with no attitude; the pitying or affectionate 'little' is a different sense.
'Young, immature' of children and animals states an age; the tender or belittling diminutive belongs to the separate 'arouses feelings' sense, and the gloss is binding.
'Anew' marks repetition and nothing more; whatever weariness a sentence carries ('never be embarrassed again') comes from the rest of it.
A unit of time carries no stance toward anything.
'Our own day' as an era is a plain period label; the disdain in the sentence sits in 'false' and 'dead-alive', not in 'day'.
A point or period in time, described without judgement.
Coming to know something by report ('I have heard that she is improved') is neutral; it neither endorses nor doubts what was heard.
Perceiving sound is the plainest of sensory verbs and takes no side.
'Let us hear all the particulars' asks for attention without any attitude toward the speaker or the matter.
The superlative marker only ranks the adjective it attaches to; 'most perfect' and 'most iniquitous' get their judgement from the adjective.
The emphatic 'a most agreeable surprise' is a formal, now dated intensifier; it strengthens but does not itself approve or condemn.
'All but' or 'almost' is a degree hedge with no stance toward what it hedges.
Early in life is a stage of age stated plainly; unlike 'youthful' or 'callow', 'young' neither flatters nor belittles.
